title: All differences of form between shells are differences of degree in a few growth ratios

fields.label: Label
fields.value: All differences of form between shells are differences of degree in a few growth ratios

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The form of any turbinate shell is fixed by a small set of factors (shape of the generating curve, its rate of growth, its rate of rotation about the pole, its rate of translation along the axis, and its inclination), and all differences of form between one shell and another are differences of degree in the relative magnitudes of these factors.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In short it is obvious that _all_ the differences of form which we observe between one shell and another are referable to matters of _degree_, depending, one and all, upon the relative magnitudes of the various factors in the complex equation to the curve.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XI, “The Logarithmic Spiral”; topic “Factors of the shell’s form”. Scope: univalve (discoid and turbinate) molluscan shells

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch11-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.71

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern shell models make the proposed factors measurable and public scans offer broad coverage. The universal 'all differences' assertion and causal sufficiency are harder to discriminate because model flexibility and omitted ornament matter.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit a generative shell model parameterizing aperture shape, expansion, rotation, translation and inclination to diverse univalve scans, then quantify unexplained shape variance and systematic residuals. The claim is supported if this parameter set reconstructs observed forms without additional qualitative mechanisms.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A flexible model can fit shapes without identifying biological causation.

Ornament, aperture remodeling and local growth changes exceed the simple parameter set.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.7
data existence: 0.85
discriminating power: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The parameter list maps onto the usual coiling model and can be fit to public shells, but all differences is stronger than a good fit to typical spires. Irregular, highly sculptured and heteromorph shells are present in the archives yet not in one harmonized morphospace. A large subset can show whether residuals are negligible, without exhausting every difference of form the claim includes.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit each univalve shell with the generating curve, its expansion, rotation about the pole, translation along the axis and inclination, and test whether residuals between shells are only quantitative. Small residuals support the claim that all form differences are of degree; structured residuals that need extra factors refute that completeness.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Open 3D coverage is uneven across living and fossil univalves.

Sculpture, aperture deviations and uncoiling may sit outside the listed factors, so the residual test depends on how the generating curve is defined.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.5
analysis feasibility: 0.6
data existence: 0.65
discriminating power: 0.55
